title: Supreme Court Opens Door on Bengal Voter Roll Purge Claims
excerpt: India's top court tells Mamata Banerjee's TMC to file fresh pleas where SIR deletions exceeded BJP's winning margins
body:
India's Supreme Court on May 11 told former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee and her Trinamool Congress that they may file fresh applications where voter deletions during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls exceeded the BJP's victory margins — a significant procedural opening just one week after the BJP swept Bengal's state elections.

**What TMC argued before the bench:**
Senior advocate and TMC MP Kalyan Banerjee argued that large-scale deletions from voter rolls had influenced results in at least 31 Assembly seats, where the margin of victory was lower than the number of names removed during the adjudication process. He cited the Jangipara constituency, where the BJP won by just 862 votes while over 5,000 voters had been deleted from the rolls — far exceeding that margin. He also submitted that the overall vote difference between the BJP and the TMC stood at nearly 32 lakh votes, while appeals against deletions exceeded 35 lakh.

**How the court and Election Commission responded:**
The CJI-led bench clarified that grievances relating to election outcomes and the alleged impact of voter deletions would require a separate interlocutory application. The Election Commission opposed the submissions, arguing that election disputes must be addressed through election petitions as provided under law, and that every grievance connected to the SIR process could not be litigated separately. Senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy warned the court that appellate tribunals handling voter roll disputes could take nearly four years to dispose of all pending appeals.

**The broader stakes in Bengal:**
Having secured 207 seats in the 294-member West Bengal Assembly — which recorded a record voter turnout above 92 per cent — the BJP decisively defeated the TMC, which managed only 80 seats and lost power after 15 years. The BJP had linked the SIR exercise to its campaign against illegal immigration across Bengal's long Bangladesh border, while the TMC alleged it disproportionately affected poor and marginalised voters.

**What to watch next:**
Whether Banerjee files the fresh interlocutory applications — and how the Supreme Court bench responds — will determine if India's highest court scrutinises the SIR's role in reshaping Bengal's political map.
nri_angle: For Indian-Americans with roots in West Bengal, this case raises foundational questions about whether voter roll purges can be used as a tool of political disenfranchisement — a debate that resonates deeply in communities familiar with voting rights battles.
author: Diaspora Desk
